intro: Paderewski recorded the Nocturne in F♯ major, Op. 15 No. 2, in London in January 1937, twenty years after his New York recording of it. The session took place shortly before his appearance on cinema screens in Moonlight Sonata.

sections.label: A · Decorated melody in F♯ major
sections.mNote: The left hand moves between low bass notes and chords.

sections.label: B · Doppio movimento, sotto voce
sections.mNote: The right hand plays a dotted melody and rapid notes together.

sections.label: C · Slow opening melody again
sections.mNote: The opening upbeat returns after the quick figures stop.

sections.label: D · F♯ major, closing flourishes
sections.mNote: Descending groups of small notes, marked smorzando.

cues.title: Opening, left-hand accompaniment
cues.text: The left hand plays a repeated figure of low bass, higher note, chord and higher note again. Above it, the right-hand melody holds long notes and moves into quick flourishes. The opening marking is sostenuto, sustained.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, upbeat and bars 1–4. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Doppio movimento section
cues.text: The right hand plays a dotted melody with a busy line underneath it, and the left hand jumps below both. Doppio movimento doubles the pace. The marking sotto voce asks for a subdued beginning.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 25–32. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the Larghetto
cues.text: The quick figures slow and thin out. After a pause, the opening melody returns at its first tempo. Chopin writes new ornaments into the reprise, and runs of small notes descend to the final F♯.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–62: slowing, pause, a Tempo and the decorated closing section. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Moonlight Sonata, film, 1937
cues.text: In February 1937 Moonlight Sonata brought Paderewski into British cinemas. He played himself in a romance involving a forced landing and a Swedish baroness. The camera also stayed on him at the piano for Beethoven’s slow movement and his own Minuet.
cues.evidence: The film opens on 11 February 1937: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonlight_Sonata_(film). Chicago Film Archives describes its preserved performance excerpts: https://collections.chicagofilmarchives.org/Detail/objects/2737

cues.title: Closing descent, bars 60–62
cues.text: Groups of small notes run down through the F♯ harmony. Chopin marks the final descent smorzando (dying away). The bass ends on a low F♯, with A♯ held above it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 60–62, including the smorzando descent and final F♯–A♯. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
